name: James Webb Space Telescope

hotspots.name: Primary mirror
hotspots.details: Webb's primary mirror is made of 18 hexagonal beryllium segments that work together as a single 6.5-meter mirror. Each segment sits on a hexapod that can adjust it in six degrees of freedom, plus a centre actuator for radius of curvature, so the 18 segments can be aligned to act as one mirror.

hotspots.name: Secondary mirror
hotspots.details: The secondary mirror takes the light collected by the primary mirror and sends it on toward Webb's instruments. It is moveable and can be adjusted to focus the telescope.

hotspots.name: Secondary-mirror support struts
hotspots.details: Three long struts form a tripod that holds the secondary mirror in front of the primary. After launch, deploying the telescope included unfolding and latching this secondary-mirror tripod into place.

hotspots.name: Sunshield
hotspots.details: The largest structure on Webb is its sunshade, about the size of a tennis court, which must shield the deployed primary mirror and the tower that holds the secondary. It has five layers rather than one thick sheet: each successive layer is cooler than the one below, heat radiates out from between the layers, and the vacuum between them is a very good insulator.

hotspots.name: Integrated Science Instrument Module (ISIM)
hotspots.details: The Integrated Science Instrument Module sits behind the primary mirror and holds Webb's four science instruments: the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), the Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec), the Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI), and the Fine Guidance Sensor / Near-Infrared Imager and Slitless Spectrograph (FGS/NIRISS).

hotspots.name: Spacecraft bus
hotspots.details: The spacecraft bus provides the support functions for the observatory. It houses six major subsystems: electrical power, attitude control, communications, command and data handling, propulsion, and thermal control.

hotspots.name: Solar array
hotspots.details: The solar array was the first major deployment after launch, about 30 minutes after liftoff, so Webb could start making electricity from sunlight and stop draining its battery. It faces the Sun and powers the observatory.

hotspots.name: High-gain antenna
hotspots.details: Webb sends science and engineering data to Earth using a high-frequency radio transmitter. Large radio antennas in NASA's Deep Space Network receive the signals and forward them to the Webb Science and Operations Center at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore.

hotspots.name: Momentum trim tab
hotspots.details: The momentum trim tab balances the pressure that sunlight (photons) exerts on Webb's sunshield. It works like a trim flap in sailing. The flap is not adjustable on orbit.

hotspots.name: Star trackers
hotspots.details: Star trackers use guide stars for coarse pointing of the telescope. Their data lets the alignment and control system point Webb so a target appears in the field of view of the intended instrument. Once an observation has started, the Fine Guidance Sensor in the ISIM compensates for small drifts.

hotspots.name: Aft-Optics Subsystem
hotspots.details: The Aft-Optics Subsystem contains the fixed tertiary mirror and the fine steering mirror. Its most prominent feature is a central baffle that protrudes from the centre of the primary mirror and keeps stray light from entering Webb's optics.

hotspots.name: Deployable tower
hotspots.details: A telescoping tower separates the spacecraft bus from the telescope. After launch it was extended 1.22 metres so that the rest of sunshield deployment could proceed, thermally isolating the cold telescope from the warm bus.
